Back: `sealed interface PaymentFailure permits PaymentMissing, InvalidPayment` allows only the listed subtypes. Each permitted subtype must choose its own policy: `final` (no further subtypes; records are implicitly final), `sealed` (restricts its own subtypes) or `non-sealed` (open to anyone again). The hierarchy is closed and known at compile time.

Front: Why use a sealed hierarchy with an exhaustive `switch`, and why avoid `default`?
Back: `switch (failure) { case PaymentMissing m -> 404; case InvalidPayment i -> 400; }` compiles without `default` because the compiler knows every permitted subtype. Add a new subtype and every such switch stops compiling until it's handled. A `default` hides that. Unlike an enum, each variant can carry its own data (`id`, `reason`). Put a guarded case like `case InvalidPayment i when i.reason().isBlank()` before the general case.

Front: How does `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler` turn PaymentNotFoundException into a 404, and why not handle it in the service?
Back: The service throws `PaymentNotFoundException(id)`; the global handler catches it for every controller and returns `ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(new ApiError(404, "Not Found", ex.getMessage(), request.getRequestURI()))`. Without it the client gets 500. The service and exception stay HTTP-free: no try/catch returning null, no ResponseEntity or HttpStatus there. Mapping a failure to a status code belongs to the web layer.
